title: Bodyweight squat setup
content: Start the squat with feet about shoulder width, weight balanced across the whole foot, and the trunk braced without holding the breath. For smart mirror coaching, prioritize a repeatable stance and controlled tempo before adding volume. The user should descend only as far as they can keep the heels down, knees tracking with the feet, and the torso controlled.
source_title: A Biomechanical Review of the Squat Exercise

title: Squat depth should follow control
content: Squat depth is a coaching variable, not a fixed rule. A deeper squat can increase knee and hip demand, so beginners or users with knee limitation should first use a depth that preserves knee alignment, trunk control, and pain-free movement. If the mirror sees stability drop near the bottom, cue a smaller range before increasing reps.
source_title: A Biomechanical Review of the Squat Exercise

title: Knee valgus during squat
content: If the knees collapse inward during the descent or ascent, reduce depth or speed and cue the user to keep the knees moving in the same direction as the toes. The correction should be simple on the mirror: slow down, keep the whole foot grounded, and push the knees gently outward without forcing an extreme stance.
source_title: Dynamic Knee Valgus and Injury Risk Review

title: Heel lift in squat
content: A heel lift during squat often signals that the user is losing balance, moving too fast, or using a range that exceeds their current ankle mobility and control. Cue a smaller range, slower descent, and pressure through the midfoot and heel. For ankle limitation, use a reduced depth and avoid turning the movement into a forward knee dive.
source_title: The Influence of Ankle Mobility and Foot Stability on Landing Mechanics

title: Trunk collapse in squat
content: When the trunk collapses or the back rounds aggressively, the next cue should be about control, not maximal depth. Ask the user to brace lightly, keep the chest and pelvis moving together, and stop the descent before the trunk position breaks. If back pain appears, reduce the exercise demand and choose a safer regression.
source_title: WHO Low Back Pain Fact Sheet

title: Slow tempo squat cue
content: For unstable squats, the first correction is often tempo. Cue the user to lower for about two seconds, pause briefly only if stable, and stand up without bouncing. Slower tempo gives the mirror more consistent frames and gives the user time to correct knee tracking and trunk control before adding repetitions.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Box squat regression cue
content: If the user cannot control depth or knee alignment, use a box squat target or imagine sitting toward a chair. This limits range, improves consistency, and gives a clear external cue. Keep the target high enough that the user can stand without knee pain or trunk collapse, then gradually lower it as control improves.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Squat knee pain stop rule
content: If the user reports sharp knee pain, sudden catching, giving way, or worsening pain during squats, the mirror should not encourage more reps. Stop the set, reduce intensity, and recommend professional evaluation if symptoms persist. For mild discomfort, lower depth and speed first, but do not increase volume in the same session.
source_title: Patellofemoral Pain Clinical Practice Guideline

title: Squat back pain stop rule
content: For back limitation, squat coaching should emphasize pain-free control rather than perfect posture claims. If back pain is sharp, radiating, or worsening, stop the movement and avoid adding load or speed. If discomfort is mild, reduce depth, slow the tempo, and use a smaller set while monitoring whether symptoms settle.
source_title: WHO Guideline for Chronic Primary Low Back Pain

title: Squat progression rule
content: Progress squat volume only after the user completes the planned reps with stable knee tracking, controlled depth, and no pain warning. A simple progression is adding one to two reps per set or one extra set, not both at once. If form score drops in the last third of the set, keep the same load next time.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Squat regression for knee limitation
content: For a user with knee limitation or repeated knee valgus, use shallow squats, box squats, or sit-to-stand patterns before full-depth squats. The goal is to train alignment and confidence without chasing depth. Keep reps moderate and rest long enough that fatigue does not turn into repeated poor knee control.
source_title: Patellofemoral Pain Clinical Practice Guideline

title: Squat post-workout feedback
content: After a squat session, useful feedback should mention completed reps, the main control issue, a reason, and the next action. If knees drifted inward, tell the user the pattern can increase knee demand and that the next session should use slower tempo or smaller depth. Keep the feedback actionable rather than technical.
source_title: A Biomechanical Review of the Squat Exercise

title: Whole-foot pressure in squat
content: A stable squat usually keeps pressure distributed across the whole foot rather than rolling strongly to the toes or inside edge. The mirror can cue the user to feel heel, big toe, and little toe contact. This helps the knee and hip share the movement and gives a simple correction when balance is inconsistent.
source_title: A Biomechanical Review of the Squat Exercise

title: Beginner squat volume
content: For a beginner smart mirror plan, squat volume should start conservatively: one to three sets with enough rest to keep movement quality. Do not increase reps if the user repeatedly shows knee valgus, heel lift, or trunk collapse. Movement quality should decide progression before the weekly plan increases total squat work.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Squat fatigue quality rule
content: When squat form deteriorates near the end of a set, the safer coaching decision is to stop or rest, not to push through for a number. Fatigue can change knee, hip, and trunk control. For weekly adjustment, repeated late-set errors mean maintain or reduce volume until the user completes reps with consistent control.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Lunge setup
content: A basic lunge should start with a stable split stance, upright but relaxed trunk, and the front knee tracking in the direction of the toes. The user should lower under control and stop before balance or knee alignment breaks. For smart mirror coaching, consistent step length and controlled return matter more than chasing depth.
source_title: Patellofemoral Joint Loading During Forward and Backward Lunge

title: Forward lunge knee overload
content: Forward lunges can create higher patellofemoral demand than some backward lunge variations. If the user has anterior knee discomfort or poor knee control, the mirror should reduce depth, shorten the set, or choose a reverse lunge style. Do not simply cue knees behind toes; use pain-free range and controlled alignment.
source_title: Patellofemoral Joint Loading During Forward and Backward Lunge

title: Lunge knee valgus
content: When the front knee drops inward during a lunge, the next cue should be simple: slow the descent, keep the knee lined with the second or third toe, and reduce depth if alignment is lost. If the pattern repeats under fatigue, lower volume for the next set instead of increasing reps.
source_title: Dynamic Knee Valgus and Injury Risk Review

title: Lunge trunk lean
content: Excessive trunk lean can shift demand and make balance harder, especially for beginners. A small forward lean can be normal, but the user should avoid collapsing or twisting. Mirror coaching should cue a tall chest, ribs stacked over pelvis, and smaller range. If back discomfort appears, regress the exercise.
source_title: WHO Low Back Pain Fact Sheet

title: Shorter lunge step cue
content: If the user wobbles, overreaches, or cannot return smoothly, shorten the lunge step and reduce depth. A shorter step makes the movement easier to control and helps the mirror capture a repeatable pattern. Once balance and knee tracking improve, step length can be gradually increased within pain-free range.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Reverse lunge regression
content: For knee-sensitive users, reverse lunges can be a useful regression because they often feel easier to control than forward lunges. Cue the user to step back softly, keep the front foot planted, and rise by pressing through the front foot. If knee pain still appears, reduce depth or change exercise.
source_title: Patellofemoral Joint Loading During Forward and Backward Lunge

title: Lunge balance stop rule
content: If the user repeatedly loses balance during lunges, the mirror should stop the set or switch to supported split squats. Balance loss increases fall risk and makes posture feedback unreliable. The next action should be hand support, smaller range, or a slower split-stance pattern rather than more repetitions.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Lunge knee pain rule
content: Sharp knee pain, sudden instability, or worsening discomfort during lunges should stop the exercise. For mild discomfort, reduce depth and use a reverse or supported variation. The weekly plan should not increase lunge volume when knee pain warnings or repeated knee valgus are recorded.
source_title: Patellofemoral Pain Clinical Practice Guideline

title: Lunge progression rule
content: Progress lunges by improving control first, then increasing reps, then adding range or load. A user should complete both sides with similar balance and knee tracking before progression. If one side repeatedly shows poorer control, keep the weaker side at a lower range and use coaching lines that mention side-to-side quality.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Supported split squat regression
content: When dynamic lunges are too difficult, a supported split squat is a simpler regression. Keep the feet in a split stance, hold a stable surface if needed, and move up and down without stepping. This preserves lower-body training while reducing balance demand and making knee alignment easier to coach.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Lunge post-workout feedback
content: Post-lunge feedback should report whether both sides were controlled, whether the knee tracked well, and what to do next. If balance errors occurred, recommend slower tempo and supported reps next session. If knee discomfort appeared, advise reduced depth and no intensity increase until the user completes pain-free reps.
source_title: Patellofemoral Joint Loading During Forward and Backward Lunge

title: Lunge foot pressure
content: In a lunge, the front foot should stay grounded so the user can press through the whole foot when standing. If the heel lifts or the foot rolls inward, reduce range and slow the movement. This cue is easier for a mirror user to follow than detailed joint-angle instructions.
source_title: The Influence of Ankle Mobility and Foot Stability on Landing Mechanics

title: Beginner lunge volume
content: Beginner lunge programming should start with small sets and enough rest to preserve side-to-side control. Lunges challenge strength and balance together, so adding too much volume quickly can lower quality. Use fewer reps per side and progress only when both sides keep stable knee tracking and controlled return.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Ankle limitation during lunge
content: Ankle discomfort or limited dorsiflexion can make lunges unstable and may encourage heel lift or knee collapse. If the mirror detects repeated ankle-side instability, reduce depth, use support, and choose controlled split squats before dynamic lunges. Do not add speed when ankle control is poor.
source_title: Ankle Stability and Landing Mechanics Study

title: Lunge slow return cue
content: A common lunge error is dropping down under control but pushing back quickly with poor alignment. Cue the user to return slowly enough that the front knee stays aligned and the trunk does not twist. If the return phase causes repeated errors, reduce reps and rest longer before the next set.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Pushup setup
content: A standard pushup should use a firm hand position, active shoulder support, and a straight line from head through trunk to legs. For mirror coaching, the first goal is controlled body-line movement, not maximal depth. If the user cannot keep trunk alignment, regress to an incline or knee-supported variation.
source_title: Shoulder Electromyography Activity During Push-up Variations

title: Pushup body line
content: Pushup coaching should watch for the hips sagging or piking. A poor body line usually means the set is too hard or fatigue is high. Cue the user to brace the trunk, squeeze the legs lightly, and choose an incline if alignment breaks before the target reps.
source_title: Shoulder Electromyography Activity During Push-up Variations

title: Pushup elbow flare
content: If the elbows flare sharply out to the side, shoulder demand can increase and control may drop. Cue the user to place hands under or slightly wider than shoulders and let elbows angle back naturally rather than straight sideways. If shoulder discomfort appears, reduce depth or use an incline variation.
source_title: Shoulder Electromyography Activity During Push-up Variations

title: Pushup shoulder shrug
content: A shoulder shrug during pushups may indicate poor scapular control or fatigue. The mirror should cue the user to press the floor away and keep the neck relaxed. If the user cannot control shoulder position, switch to an incline pushup so the movement remains trainable without forcing painful reps.
source_title: Shoulder Electromyography Activity During Push-up Variations

title: Pushup partial depth under fatigue
content: If pushup depth shortens rapidly across reps, treat it as fatigue rather than failure of effort. The next coaching action is to stop the set, rest, or regress the angle. Adding more reps while depth and trunk control disappear will not support good technique for a smart mirror beginner plan.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Incline pushup regression
content: Incline pushups reduce the amount of body weight the user must press and are a simple regression for shoulder, trunk, or strength limitations. Cue the user to use a stable surface, keep the body line straight, and move slowly. Progress by lowering the incline only after reps are controlled and pain-free.
source_title: Shoulder Electromyography Activity During Push-up Variations

title: Push the floor away cue
content: For shoulder control in pushups, a useful cue is to push the floor away at the top while keeping the neck long. This encourages active support through the shoulder girdle without adding complex anatomy language. If the cue does not improve control, reduce difficulty with an incline.
source_title: Shoulder Electromyography Activity During Push-up Variations

title: Pushup shoulder pain stop rule
content: Sharp shoulder pain, sudden weakness, or pain that worsens across pushup reps should stop the exercise. The mirror should not recommend more volume that day. Use an incline or different exercise only if symptoms are mild and settle quickly; otherwise advise the user to stop and seek professional guidance if persistent.
source_title: Rotator Cuff Clinical Practice Guideline

title: Pushup wrist discomfort
content: Pushups can irritate wrists for some users because the hands bear load in extension. If wrist pain appears, stop or switch to a pain-free hand position such as handles or fists only if safe and stable. Do not force full pushups when wrist pain changes the user's hand support.
source_title: Wrist and Hand Loading During Push-up Study

title: Pushup progression rule
content: Progress pushups by first increasing clean reps at the current incline, then lowering the incline, and only later increasing sets. If trunk sag, elbow flare, or shoulder shrug appears late in the set, hold the current level. A weekly plan should not progress pushups when quality drops before target reps.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Knee pushup caution
content: Knee pushups can reduce difficulty, but the user still needs a straight line from shoulders to knees and active trunk control. If the hips drop or shoulders shrug, an incline pushup may be clearer for mirror coaching. Choose the regression that produces the cleanest repeatable movement, not the hardest version.
source_title: Shoulder Electromyography Activity During Push-up Variations

title: Pushup post-workout feedback
content: Post-pushup coaching should tell the user how many reps were completed, whether trunk and shoulder control held, and what version to use next. If alignment broke down, recommend an incline next time. If control was steady and pain-free, maintain or slightly increase reps rather than changing multiple variables.
source_title: Shoulder Electromyography Activity During Push-up Variations

title: Pushup breathing and tempo
content: The user should not rush pushups just to reach a count. A steady lower and controlled press gives better movement quality and more reliable mirror feedback. Cue breathing normally, keeping the trunk braced without breath-holding. If tempo speeds up and form drops, end the set or regress.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Beginner pushup volume
content: Beginner pushup volume should start low enough that the user can finish with consistent alignment. One to three sets of a regression is better than repeated failed full pushups. The plan should use the version that allows clean reps and gradually increase difficulty after stable completion.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Pushup low back warning
content: If pushups repeatedly create low back discomfort or the hips sag, the exercise is too difficult for the current setup. Reduce demand with an incline and cue a shorter set. Do not frame this as a spinal diagnosis; treat it as a movement control issue and stop if pain is sharp or worsening.
source_title: WHO Low Back Pain Fact Sheet

title: Jumping jack setup
content: A jumping jack should start tall with soft knees, relaxed shoulders, and enough space around the user. The goal is rhythmic whole-body movement, not maximal speed. For beginners, the mirror should prioritize landing softly, keeping the feet under control, and maintaining breathing before increasing time or tempo.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Soft landing cue
content: For jumping jacks, the key safety cue is soft, quiet landing with knees slightly bent. Loud or stiff landings suggest poor shock absorption or fatigue. The mirror should cue a slower rhythm, smaller step width, or a low-impact step jack if landing quality drops.
source_title: Utility of Jumping and Landing Variables as Predictors of Injury Risk

title: Stiff knee landing
content: Landing with locked or stiff knees during jumping jacks can increase impact and reduce control. Cue the user to land softly with a slight knee bend and to slow down. If the user cannot soften the landing after cueing, switch to step jacks or marching until control improves.
source_title: Utility of Jumping and Landing Variables as Predictors of Injury Risk

title: Ankle rolling during jacks
content: If the feet roll inward or outward during jumping jacks, reduce speed and range. Poor foot control can make repeated landings less stable. A low-impact step jack keeps the aerobic pattern while removing repeated hops, which is a better choice for users with ankle limitation or unstable landings.
source_title: The Influence of Ankle Mobility and Foot Stability on Landing Mechanics

title: Shoulder tension during jacks
content: Shoulder tension during jumping jacks often appears when the user raises the arms too high or moves too fast. Cue a smaller arm range and relaxed neck. If shoulder pain is present, use lower arm swings while keeping the stepping rhythm. Aerobic benefit does not require forcing overhead motion.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Step jack regression
content: A step jack is the main regression for jumping jacks. The user steps one foot out and in while moving the arms, avoiding repeated jumping. Use it when landing is noisy, balance is poor, knee or ankle limitation is present, or measurement quality is low. Progress back to hops only after rhythm and control are steady.
source_title: CDC Physical Activity Guidelines and Recommended Strategies

title: Reduce range before speed
content: When jumping jacks look uncontrolled, reduce range before increasing speed. Smaller steps and lower arm height let the user maintain rhythm without losing posture. If the user keeps good landing and breathing for the planned duration, speed can increase later in the weekly plan.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Cardio red flag rule
content: Stop jumping jacks if the user reports dizziness, chest pain, severe shortness of breath, or feels faint. The mirror should not encourage finishing the timer in those cases. Use clear safety language, advise rest, and recommend professional help if symptoms are severe or do not resolve.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Jumping jack knee or ankle pain
content: If knee or ankle pain appears during jumping jacks, stop hopping and switch to step jacks or marching. Repeated impacts should not continue through sharp or worsening joint pain. The next plan should lower impact and rebuild rhythm before increasing duration.
source_title: CDC Adding Physical Activity as an Adult

title: Jumping jack progression rule
content: Progress jumping jacks by increasing duration or rhythm only when the user keeps soft landings and steady breathing. Do not increase both time and speed in the same week for beginners. If the final seconds show stiff landings or arm tension, keep the same duration next time.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Marching regression
content: Marching in place is a lower-impact substitute when step jacks are still too difficult or the camera cannot reliably track jumping. It preserves aerobic intent while reducing landing demand. Use it for low measurement confidence, balance problems, or joint discomfort, then progress to step jacks when steady.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Jumping jack post-workout feedback
content: After jumping jacks, feedback should mention duration or count, breathing rhythm, landing quality, and next action. If landings were stiff or ankle control was poor, recommend step jacks next time. If the user finished with soft landings and steady rhythm, a small duration increase is reasonable.
source_title: Utility of Jumping and Landing Variables as Predictors of Injury Risk

title: Breathing rhythm for jacks
content: Jumping jacks should feel rhythmic enough that the user can keep breathing. If the user holds breath, rushes, or loses coordination, lower the tempo. This is especially important for beginners and weight-management plans, where consistency and safe aerobic volume matter more than high speed.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Beginner jumping jack volume
content: For beginners, short intervals of jumping jacks or step jacks are better than long sets that degrade landing quality. Start with manageable duration, rest enough to restore rhythm, and increase total time gradually. If measurement quality is low, choose a slower low-impact option so coaching remains reliable.
source_title: CDC Adding Physical Activity as an Adult

title: Low measurement quality for jacks
content: Jumping jacks can be hard for a camera to track if the user is partly out of frame or moving too fast. Low measurement confidence should be mentioned in coaching. The next action is to slow down, center the body in frame, or use step jacks until the mirror can provide reliable feedback.
source_title: Smart Mirror Measurement Quality Rule

title: Standing knee raise setup
content: A standing knee raise should start tall with a stable support option nearby if needed. The user lifts one knee without leaning back or rushing. For mirror coaching, balance and trunk control are the main goals. A smaller lift is acceptable if the user can keep posture and breathing steady.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Knee raise trunk control
content: If the trunk leans backward during knee raises, the user may be lifting too high or too fast. Cue a smaller knee height, tall posture, and slow return. The goal is controlled hip flexion with balance, not maximal range. If back discomfort appears, reduce height or switch to marching.
source_title: WHO Low Back Pain Fact Sheet

title: Knee raise hip hiking
content: A common knee raise error is hiking the hip or tilting the trunk to get the knee higher. This reduces control and can make balance worse. Cue the user to lift lower, keep the pelvis level, and pause only if stable. Quality matters more than height for this exercise.
source_title: Hip Flexor Activation During Common Exercises

title: Knee raise loss of balance
content: If the user loses balance during knee raises, the mirror should reduce challenge immediately. Use fingertip support, lower knee height, or slow marching. Balance errors should not be pushed through for extra reps, especially with older adults or users reporting dizziness.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Knee raise fast drop
content: Dropping the foot quickly after a knee raise reduces control and may challenge balance more than intended. Cue the user to lower the foot quietly and stand tall between reps. If control drops late in the set, reduce reps or add rest before switching sides.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Supported knee raise cue
content: For balance limitations, supported knee raises are the first regression. The user can place one or two fingers on a stable surface while lifting the knee. This keeps the exercise useful for hip and trunk control while lowering fall risk and making the movement easier to track.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Marching regression for knee raise
content: If single-leg knee raises are unstable, use slow marching in place. Marching keeps a similar pattern but reduces balance time on one leg. Cue small steps, tall posture, and quiet foot contact. Progress back to knee raises when the user can march without trunk sway or loss of rhythm.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Knee raise dizziness rule
content: Stop knee raises if the user feels dizzy, faint, or unable to maintain balance. The mirror should recommend sitting or resting rather than continuing the set. For future sessions, use supported marching or a seated variation until the user can move safely without balance symptoms.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Hip or back pain in knee raise
content: Sharp hip or back pain during knee raises should stop the exercise. Mild tightness can be handled by lowering knee height and slowing the tempo, but pain that worsens should not be trained through. The next plan should use smaller range or marching rather than higher knee targets.
source_title: WHO Low Back Pain Fact Sheet

title: Knee raise progression rule
content: Progress knee raises by improving control before increasing height or speed. A user should complete reps with quiet foot placement and stable trunk before adding time or alternating faster. If balance errors appear late in the set, keep the same volume and add support next time.
source_title: ACSM Progression Models in Resistance Training

title: Seated knee raise regression
content: A seated knee raise is a useful regression when standing balance is unsafe. It keeps the hip flexion pattern while removing fall risk. Cue tall posture, slow lifting, and controlled lowering. Use this option when dizziness, poor balance, or low confidence makes standing knee raises unsuitable.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Knee raise post-workout feedback
content: After knee raises, feedback should focus on balance, trunk control, and whether the user completed reps without rushing. If balance was unstable, recommend support or marching next time. If control was steady, the next plan can add a small number of reps or a slightly longer hold.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Knee raise side-to-side quality
content: Knee raises should be checked on both sides because one side may show worse balance or smaller range. The mirror should not average away a clear side difference. If one side is unstable, coach the user to use support and lower height on that side until control improves.
source_title: WHO Guidelines on Physical Activity and Sedentary Behaviour

title: Beginner knee raise volume
content: For beginners, knee raises can be used as a low-impact habit and balance exercise. Start with small sets, slow tempo, and support if needed. The plan should progress only when the user finishes with steady posture and no dizziness. More speed is not the first progression.
source_title: Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans, 2nd edition

title: Low measurement quality for knee raise
content: If the mirror cannot see the full body or confidence is low, knee raise feedback should mention measurement limits. The next action is to center the user in frame, slow down, and use a clear pause at the top. Do not overinterpret balance or range when the camera signal is poor.
source_title: Smart Mirror Measurement Quality Rule
